Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

vignette: The night it unraveled began in their shared kitchen. His partner had followed him from the living room, voice rising over a debate about shared expenses, then circling back to how Rohan kept his phone locked. The conversation had circled the same controlling points for hours. When Rohan tried to step toward the door, the other man grabbed his wrist, shoved him against the cabinets, and pinned him there. Rohan remembered the heavy, sour smell of sweat radiating off his partner's chest, the exact words repeated like a metronome: "You're not leaving. Just sit and listen." His partner's hands left bruises that mapped his ribs for weeks, but it was the heat, the rhythm of the voice, and the specific, dismissive phrases that remained etched in his attention. Weeks later, the smell of a crowded street made Rohan's breath catch. He found himself holding his own breath, waiting for that heavy, musky scent of body odor to pass. The shop he owned offered little refuge. When a regular customer leaned across the counter to complain about a delayed shipment, talking over him and insisting on his own terms, Rohan's vision would blur and the kitchen cabinets would materialize behind his eyes. Something in his surroundings would instantly bring back the full memory without warning. He would drop a stack of invoices, his hands trembling, as a white-hot wave of rage flooded his chest. Sometimes there was no image at all. He would simply lie awake, his heart hammering against his ribs, carrying the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear picture of why he felt like a cornered animal. He noticed it was harder to feel safe at night than during the day. The silence of his apartment felt like a trap. He lay awake, listening to the refrigerator hum, turning his head toward the door with every footstep in the hallway, unable to fall or stay asleep. During daylight, he walked with his shoulders hunched, scanning every entrance. He noticed strangers approaching him on the sidewalk, even when they were simply walking past or heading toward the crosswalk, and his stomach would tighten. He told himself they were just moving through their days, but his body kept reacting as if he were still pinned against those cabinets. He stopped answering the shop's back door, preferring to let orders go unfulfilled rather than face an uninvited knock. When customers brought up topics about boundaries, control, or past relationships, Rohan would abruptly close the register, wash his hands repeatedly, and sit on a stool until they left. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, replaying the moment his wrist was grabbed and wondering why he hadn't pulled away sooner. He came to believe he could not rely on himself to protect his own body. His own pulse, his own trembling hands, felt like traitors in a room that was completely safe. Months had passed since he moved out, but the weight of those nights settled heavily on his shoulders. His current partner had noticed how Rohan flinched when reaching for the same shelf, and how Rohan insisted on sleeping in the guest room with a chair wedged under the doorknob. Rohan had come to dread the shop floor, the sudden conversations, the way his own nervous system seemed to short-circuit without permission. He sat in the intake office now, fingers tracing the frayed edge of his jeans, unsure if he could explain why a simple customer service interaction left him gasping. What he hoped for was a way to quiet the constant alarms in his head, to walk into his store without bracing for impact, to sleep through the night without checking the locks. What he feared most was that he would always be waiting for the other shoe to drop, that his own body would never stop warning him of a danger that was over.
